Background
Femoral and acetabular components often must be removed during revision total hip
arthroplasty (THA).
Safe implant removal is critical to subsequent reconstruction.
Iatrogenic injury can be avoided via knowledge of relevant anatomy and extensile approaches.

Background
The successful removal of well-fixed failed THA components is an essential initial step in
revision total hip arthroplasty (rTHA). Despite improvements in technique and
instrumentation, component removal remains a demanding and time-consuming aspect
of revision surgery, even for a prepared and experienced team.1 A systematic approach
to component removal is crucial to avoid unnecessary damage to bone and surrounding
structures and sets the stage for subsequent reconstruction. The goal of rTHA is to
reproduce, as closely as possible, the form and function of the native hip joint; this
becomes increasingly difficult with bone loss, whether iatrogenically induced or because
of underlying pathology. Therefore, every effort should be made to preserve host bone
stock. With this goal in mind, a stepwise approach to rTHA is paramount. The keys to
safe component removal involve a comprehensive understanding of the mode of failure,
a detailed preoperative plan, technical expertise, and patience.2
Pathogenesis
Conditions that necessitate removal of femoral or acetabular components include the
following3:
Recurrent dislocation because of malpositioned components
Mechanical loosening, including aseptic failure
Periprosthetic joint infection
Periprosthetic fracture
Component impingement
Limb-length discrepancy that is symptomatic

Preoperative Planning
Obtain prior surgical records.
Prior surgical records can provide information on the surgical approach, implant type, and
implant size.
All component identifiers (component stickers) should be acquired and determined if
possible because surgical reports may be inaccurate.4
Industry representatives should be involved preoperatively to confirm the existing implant
compatibilities with planned revision implants if retention of components is being
considered.
Obtain imaging and diagnostic studies
Good preoperative imaging studies help identify components that are well fixed and help
evaluate bone stock available for rTHA.
Preoperative radiographic views should include the following:
Biplanar radiographs of the entire implant and the joints above and below the components,
including the entire cement mantle if cemented components are present
The acetabular and femoral component position and fixation should be assessed, and any
radiolucent lines about the components or any bony deficits should be noted to aid in
reconstructive planning.
Greater trochanteric anatomy and bony quality should be scrutinized because they may
have a direct effect on the ability to reconstruct the abductor mechanism and limit
postoperative instability.
Eccentric polyethylene wear and osteolysis should be noted. The presence of osteolytic
lesions about the pelvis and femur must be identified to prepare for unanticipated bone
loss and/or obtain advanced imaging studies.
Heterotopic ossification should alert the surgeon about the possibility of more difficult
dissection and potentially increased blood loss.
Full-length femur radiographs

Systematic Approach for Reconstruction
Multiple reconstructive options must be available for rTHA to match the femoral and
acetabular defects present after removal of existing implants.
The appropriate removal instruments and surgical approach are important considerations
before rTHA.
Additional preoperative planning should account for the following:
Polyethylene liner exchange options
Revision acetabular components (even if the acetabular implant appears radiographically
stable)
Revision femoral components (even if the femoral implant appears radiographically stable)

Systematic Approach for Reconstruction
Preoperative planning begins with a detailed patient history and comprehensive physical
examination (Resource 1). A good preoperative plan should provide a clear
understanding of the reason the hip is being revised and the manner in which, step-by-
step, the revision procedures will be performed (Video 1). Attempts should be made to
obtain the original surgical procedure report to determine the manufacturer, model, and
size of the components and the finished surface of the femoral component to plan the
level of difficulty during removal. In addition, specific extraction devices for the original
implant may be available from the manufacturer and should be obtained. A complete
sequential series of plain radiographs may aid in determining the mode of implant

include proximal stress shielding, spot welding to the porous coating, an absence of a
distal pedestal, and a lack of reactive lines around the implant.
Preoperative templating can be performed with the use of acetate or digital imaging
tools but must include an assessment of the degree and location of bone defects
because this will ultimately determine the surgical plan and components that will be
used for reconstruction (Video 2; Table 1). Preparation before rTHA is imperative to
allow for consideration of each surgical step in detail, predict possible intraoperative
difficulties, and plan strategies to avoid or address complications if they arise (Video 3).
Templating also assures the appropriate surgical approach is selected and the
appropriate tools and extraction devices are available for each patient.
Advanced imaging studies (CT, MRI, or pelvic angiography) may help assess the
relationship of the implants or the retained cement to intrapelvic structures. If the
retained hardware is juxtaposed to important intrapelvic structures, a vascular or
general surgeon should be contacted to prepare for a possible retroperitoneal
dissection.

Surgical Approach and Anatomy
The approach to the hip for revision surgery should be easily extensile (Resource 2).
Although no single surgical approach may be best for all revision procedures, surgeons should
use the approach with which they are most proficient to optimize exposure and reduce
iatrogenic injury.10,11
The incision should be made through a preexisting scar if possible; however, the scar should
not dictate the surgical approach if the surgeon is unfamiliar with the approach.
Patient Positioning
After administration of anesthesia and insertion of a urinary catheter, the patient can be safely
positioned, taking care to pad bony prominences and prevent iatrogenic injury to structures
because revision THA often is longer than primary THA.
Patients can be placed in the lateral decubitus position for anterolateral and posterior
approaches.
Patients can be placed in the supine position for anterior and anterolateral approaches.
Posterior (Moore or Southern) Approach
The patient is placed in the lateral decubitus position, and the hip is exposed by splitting the
iliotibial band and the gluteus maximus muscle during superficial dissection and reflecting the

short external rotators and underlying hip capsule during deep dissection. Deliberate repair of
the posterior capsule and the external rotators is recommended to reduce the incidence of
dislocation after rTHA.12
The sciatic nerve is at risk with the extensile posterior approach. The sciatic nerve can be
identified in three distinct anatomic locations.
Exiting the sciatic notch deep to the piriformis muscle and superficial to the short external
rotators (ie, superior gemellus, obturator internus, and inferior gemellus muscles)
Superficial to the ischium, posterior and inferior to the posterior acetabular column superficial
to the quadratus femoris muscle
Deep to the femoral insertion of the gluteus maximus tendon on the posterior femur
Anterolateral (Watson-Jones or Hardinge) Approach
The patient is placed in the supine or the lateral decubitus position, and the hip is exposed by
splitting the iliotibial band and the gluteus maximus muscle during superficial dissection and
reflecting the anterior third of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles with or without a
portion of the vastus lateralis muscle during deep dissection. This approach maintains the
posterior attachments of the hip, which decreases the incidence of dislocation after rTHA.
The superior gluteal nerve is at risk during a trans-trochanteric or extensile anterolateral
approach. The superior gluteal nerve travels deep to the gluteus medius anteriorly along the
ilium, approximately 4 to 5 cm proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter.
Anterior (Modified Smith-Petersen) Approach
The patient is placed in the supine position, and the hip is exposed via the internervous plane
between the femoral and superior gluteal nerves, using the interval between the tensor fascia
latae and the sartorius muscles during superficial dissection and the gluteus medius and
rectus femoris muscles during deep dissection. This approach maintains the posterior
attachments of the hip, which decreases the incidence of dislocation after rTHA.
The femoral nerve is at risk with excessive anterior dissection and retraction and approaches
to the hip that are medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (eg, extended iliofemoral).
Extensile Bony Options
Extended greater trochanteric osteotomy (ETO)

Transfemoral (Wagner) osteotomy. Usually performed via a lateral, anterolateral, or anterior
approach (Figure 1)
The length of the transfemoral osteotomy is determined by the amount of prosthesis that is
well fixed or the distal extent of the cement column that needs to be removed. A transfemoral
osteotomy is particularly useful in patients with coronal fracture fragments or extensive
proximal bone loss.
The femur is split at the level of the greater trochanter with the use of a large osteotome. The
gluteus medius and minimus and the vastus lateralis muscles are split but remain attached to
the anterior and posterior portions of the osteotomy (Figure 1, A).
The distal extent of the osteotomy is completed by beveling the osteotomy anteriorly or
posteriorly or by making a complete transfemoral cut, booking open the proximal femur. This
portion of the osteotomy can be performed with the use of a pencil-tipped high-speed burr or
an oscillating saw (Figure 1, B).
The entire trans-trochanteric fragment is reflected anteriorly and/or posteriorly, with extreme
care not to fracture the tip of the greater trochanteric fragment (Figure 1, C). The greater
trochanter is the weakest point in the trans-trochanteric fragment.
The capsule surrounding the prosthesis is divided superiorly and inferiorly, leaving the
anterior and posterior sleeves intact and the shoulder of the prosthesis exposed.
A cerebellar-type or Charnley-type hip retractor is used to carefully retract the trans-
trochanteric fragment(s) to expose the femoral prosthesis.
The surgeon then has access to the cement-implant, cement-bone, or bone-implant interfaces
as necessary for femoral component removal.
Access to the acetabulum is attained after femoral component extraction or via anterior or
posterior dislocation of the hip. Dislocation before femoral component extraction is preferred
to avoid iatrogenic fracture of the osteotomy or the distal femur.
Preparation of the acetabulum is completed.
Before femoral component preparation, most surgeons elect to place a prophylactic cable
around the femur just distal to the osteotomy site to prevent iatrogenic femoral shaft fracture.
ETO fixation is performed with the use of looped Luque wires or metallic or nonmetallic cables
before or after final implant insertion. (Figure 1, D).

The length of the cortical window is determined by the amount of prosthesis that is well fixed
or the distal extent of the cement column that needs to be removed.13 As much as one-third
of the lateral portion of the femoral cortical circumference may be included in a cortical
window (Figures 2 and 3).
Similar to the ETO, the vastus lateralis muscle remains attached to the lateral portion of the
osteotomy at the vastus ridge; however, distally, the vastus lateralis muscle is elevated off the
linea aspera and retracted anteriorly to allow for visualization of the lateral and posterior
femoral cortex.
Drill holes are made at the corner of the window to reduce any potential stress risers that may
lead to iatrogenic femur fracture.
The drill holes are connected via an osteotome or an oscillating saw.
The surgeon may remove the cortical window with the use of an osteotome and gain limited
access to the cement-implant, cement-bone, or bone-implant interfaces as necessary for
femoral component removal. A carbide punch can be used to extract components in a
retrograde fashion.
The cortical window is temporarily held into position with the use of Farabeuf clamps during
trialing and final component placement.
The bone fragment is fixed permanently to bone after the final implant is inserted with the use
of cerclage cables or looped Luque wires.

Episiotomy
Start with the longitudinal limb of the osteotomy down the shaft of femur, creating an
episiotomy to relieve some of the tension and allow for easier disimpaction.20 Depending on
the extent of femoral component fixation, this episiotomy may allow for component extraction
without completing the osteotomy; however, it can easily be converted to an ETO.
Care must be taken to not inadvertently fracture the bone during attempted extraction after
episiotomy because a controlled break is much easier to fix than an inadvertent trochanteric
fracture.
Fixation for Osteotomy
Metallic cables, nonmetallic cables (suture or polyethylene), and wires can be used for cerclage
fixation.14
Trochanteric osteotomies can be secured with the use of a cerclage wire/claw plate construct
depending on the length of the osteotomy fragment. At least two cables typically are necessary
to provide stability.

The surgeon should be proficient with an extensile approach to the hip during revision
THA. Extensile exposure is used to ensure circumferential component visualization,
which allows for implant removal with minimal iatrogenic bone loss and reduces the risk
of periprosthetic fracture. Depending on surgeon preference, an extensile approach

The neurovascular structures at risk during rTHA and the removal of well-fixed implants
include the sciatic, superior gluteal, and femoral nerves and the femoral vasculature.
Care must be taken to avoid injury to the superior gluteal nerve while splitting the
gluteus medius muscle during a lateral approach,15 the sciatic nerve during the posterior
approach, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and the femoral nerve during the
direct anterior approach.16 If additional proximal femur exposure is required to safely
remove the component, iliopsoas release from the lesser trochanter may be considered.
To improve the ease of and outcomes of rTHA, the femoral component must be
removed with minimal bone loss, the remaining host bone must be prepared without
inadvertent perforation, and a femoral implant must be inserted concentrically with
adequate axial and rotational stability. Preoperative planning and knowledge of the
specifications of the existing femoral component, including surface coating and distance
of ongrowth, may help predict the level of difficulty of femoral component extraction.
Occasionally, osteotomies of the proximal femur are required during rTHA. An ETO is an
extensile option (Resource 2) that allows for exposure of the proximal femur via a
controlled cortical fracture and achieves the goals of improved access to the implant-
bone or implant-cement interface, concentric reaming of the distal femur in patients
with a proximal femur deformity, appropriate abductor tensioning, improved acetabular
visualization, and predictable healing of the osteotomy.17 Additional benefits of an ETO
include minimal undersizing of the femoral implants, improved initial implant stability,
and minimal risk of cortical perforation (Video 7). Preoperative imaging studies should
be used to template the planned osteotomy, including the length, which will depend on
the surgical indication. The preoperative plan also should include the type of fixation and
the amount of fixation required to repair the osteotomy. Options include metallic wires
and metallic or nonmetallic cables.18

A cortical window also is an extensile option, and the length of a cortical window is

The design principle of a proximally porous-coated noncemented stem is to achieve

osteotome for the medial calcar up to the distal most extent of the porous coating as
determined by the implant manufacturer specifications and the preoperative template. If
the medial side is blocked by a collar, a metal-cutting burr may be used to remove the
collar and gain access to the calcar. Care should be taken because osteotomes increase

universal extractor is applied to the neck of the stem. If the femoral component does not
have a lipped taper, notching of the inferior aspect of the femoral neck with the use of a

Broken Stem
A broken noncemented femoral stem is, by definition, well fixed distally. Similar to a
proximally porous-coated stem, the proximal portion of a broken stem should be
removed carefully to avoid trochanteric fracture. Depending on distal stem geometry,
options for removal include disruption of the implant-bone interface with the use of long

visualize the stem and a high-impact carbide punch strong enough to dig into the
femoral component is placed in the window to allow the impacts to drive the stem
proximally until it is no longer visualized in the window. Another more proximal window
can then be created, and the process can be repeated until the stem is able to be
extracted from the proximal portion of the femur.

Cement Removal

Cement Removal
After the implant is removed, attention is shifted to removal of the cement from the
femoral canal. This is an arduous and time-consuming task associated with considerable
surgical time and morbidity from removal of good bone stock and canal perforations.
With great care and patience, removal of cement from the femoral canal may be
accomplished via a combination of manual cement removal instruments (eg, splitter, V-
shaped osteotome, T-shaped osteotome, reverse hook, pituitary rongeur, drills and taps
designed for cement removal), motorized osteotomes, a pencil-tipped high-speed burr
to create fault lines and control cement fracture, a round high-speed burr for
metaphyseal cement, a drill, and an orthopaedic ultrasonic cement removal system that
heats and softens the polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) allowing for less troublesome
removal.25 The purported advantages of ultrasonic cement removal tools include
preservation of bone stock, ease of distal cement plug removal, tactile and auditory
feedback, and avoidance of an osteotomy.26 If the cement mantle will be retained, the
well-fixed, noninfected cement mantle can be contoured and texturized with the use of a
burr or an ultrasonic device to create space for a new femoral component that is
cemented into the existing cement mantel (ie, cement-in-cement technique);27 however,
the quality of this cement mantle if using an ultrasonic device may be inferior to a fresh
cement mantle.28 The distal cement plug may be removed in a retrograde fashion,
especially if loose, via a cortical window13 or in antegrade fashion by making a central
hole in the distal cement with the use of a drill, burr, or ultrasonic device and using a
reverse hook to extract the distal cement. If the distal cement is distal to the isthmus of
the femur, a cortical window or an ETO should be considered; alternatively, the cement
can be retained distally, and fixation can be achieved in an intact isthmus above the
retained cement to avoid the morbidity associated with removal. A final option for
intramedullary cement removal involves insertion of fresh PMMA into the existing
cement mantle and placement of an extraction rod with nuts into the new cement. After
the cement has cured, the extraction rod can be removed with the intact cement mantle,
with the assumption that the PMMA-PMMA bond is stronger than the bone-cement
interface.20

Trochanteric precautions (no active abduction) may be considered during the healing
process after an ETO.
Toe-touch weight bearing occasionally is prescribed for 8 weeks or more in patients with
major bone loss or if fixation is deemed to be at risk.
Clinical and radiographic surveillance is based on surgeon discretion but generally is
performed every 6 weeks until bony union, after which it is performed at 4 to 6 months, 1 year,
2 years, and every 2 years thereafter.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Preoperatively
Discuss the procedure with the patient to help him or her form realistic expectations.
Perform detailed preoperative templating and ensure the manufacturer representative
confirms that the correct tools will be available on the day of surgery.

Acetabular and femoral deficiencies
Osteolysis and bone loss behind well-fixed acetabular components or around proximally
porous-coated femoral implants often is underestimated on plain radiographs. A simple
polyethylene liner and femoral head exchange may progress to complete acetabular revision
if the implants prove to be loose or osteolysis extensive. A detailed preoperative plan should
include implants and equipment available for full component revision.
ETO
Bevel the distal transverse arm of the osteotomy to prevent distal fracture propagation.
Pass a cerclage wire distal to the osteotomy before femoral preparation.
Careful attention should be paid to trochanteric osteolysis and fracture risk at the vastus
ridge at the junction of the vastus lateralis and the abductor attachment into the trochanter.
With distally fixed stems and an ETO, a tight distal diaphyseal fit must be attained.
Intraoperative and/or postoperative radiographs must be obtained after the final implants in
place because intraoperative fracture rates are higher for rTHA.
An ETO can be performed in combination with proximal reduction or an angular osteotomy.
Leave the vastus muscle attached to the trochanteric fragment to provide adequate blood
supply for osseous healing and implant stability.
Femoral component removal
Define the implant-bone interface to prevent iatrogenic injury.
All the tools must be ready, with multiple backup tools in case the explant tools break.
An extensile approach should be used so the femur can be directly inspected if a cortical
perforation has occurred.
Using an intramedullary guidewire may help guide reamers into the distal femur and avoid
perforations.
Multiple trephines, one size larger and one size smaller than the dictated implant size, should
be available because trephines dull quickly and implant sizes often are dictated incorrectly.
Complete cement removal is essential. Incomplete cement removal may lead to eccentric
femoral canal reaming and cortical perforation or fracture.
Consider obtaining AP and lateral radiographs of the femur during reaming, implantation, or
at the end of the procedure to confirm the absence of a fracture distal to the tip of the
prosthesis.
All cortical perforations and potential stress risers should be bypassed by the new
prosthesis.

Intraoperative fracture: usually technique-related and avoidable
Femoral fractures are common near the greater trochanteric region and in the femoral
diaphysis during removal of well-fixed femoral implants.31
Femoral perforation and iatrogenic fracture may preclude a tight diaphyseal fit, which is

Postoperative fracture: usually related to poor bone quality or difficulty in complying with

Nonunion can occur in the setting of an ETO or a transfemoral osteotomy.17,33,34

Revision THA is associated with a higher dislocation rate than primary THA.36

disruption of the anterior and posterior columns
Occurs in 0.9% of rTHA procedures and may occur in patients with bony acetabular

Outcomes

Outcomes
With modern reconstruction techniques, survivorship free of any re-revision after aseptic
rTHA may be as high as 94%, 92%, and 88% at 2, 5, and 10 years postoperatively,
respectively. The most common reasons for re-revision after aseptic rTHA are hip
instability (52%), periprosthetic fracture (11%), femoral aseptic loosening (11%),
acetabular aseptic loosening (9%), infection (6%), polyethylene wear (3%), and other
reasons (8%).41
The incidence of infection after aseptic rTHA varies depending on the reason for revision,
host and soft-tissue status, and the time since the index procedures;42 however, it may
be as high as 8%.43
Conclusion

Conclusion
Safe component removal during rTHA beings with a detailed preoperative plan that
outlines a stepwise intraoperative approach. Regardless of intentions, implant removal
may easily turn into an hours-long process of chiseling away at a solidly fixed
component. Impatience, even for a moment, may result in catastrophic bone loss or
fracture and turn an already difficult procedure into an even more complex revision
procedure. By adhering to basic revision principles, surgeons can provide their patients
with the best likelihood of durable reconstruction with minimal morbidity.
